text: They are located in the Ferry Market in New Hope Pennsylvania which have a variety of better than fast food restaurants to sample when you either are looking for something quick or don't have the time to wait at a sit down restaurant and be served. This is a family owned business which I love supporting. All of the food was outstanding and the owner/chef Nadal and his son were very nice. They offer a wide variety of Mediterranean options and they have vegan dishes as well. They have salads, combination platters, pita sandwiches, soups, beverages and deserts. The spices they use bring out the flavor without being overbearing. Everything is homemade and is fresh. I sampled a combination platter with salad, hummus, baba ghanoush , chicken gyro, and Mediterranean salad. The portion could easily be shared by two and was a great value for the price. We also had the Mediterranean chicken platter which was equally as good and filling. They have vegan options as well. They have a counter that seats about five or you can opt for seating in other areas of the market or outside when the weather is warmer. My friends own a business in New Hope just steps away and would eat here everyday if they could.I would highly recommend them and they probably have the best Mediterranean food in New Hope.

text: Rushed my mother to Williamson medical at 1 AM this morning hoping to get relief from the writhing pain she was experiencing related to bladder cancer. Despite having only one other patient, the ER team was cold, harsh, thoughtless and entirely lacking in empathy. They were also mistaken in key parts of their diagnosis and their treatment. Based on my experience today, I would never send a relative or a friend to Williamson Medical under any circumstance imaginable. Why do these "healthcare professionals" feel they are serving their patients if they allow interminable delays (we were left for 2 hours without getting pain medication of any kind - the very reason we went in the first place) and brutish bedside manners (being moved from bed to gurney like a sack of potatoes, my mother getting screamed at during insertion of a catheter, blaming the patient for difficulty finding a vein {it took 3 tries and 3 pokes} in which to insert an IV, etc.). 10-minutes into the nurse screaming catheter insertion I heard the head nurse, Amy, finally ask my mother what her name was. Think about that. I found medical trash strewn all over the room we were in. This is 3rd world treatment and 3rd world quality care. I have great reverence for those who commit their lives to the serving and healing of strangers. I revere and feel hfriends who are ER doctors, social workers, cancer scientists. These people serve mankind and they have empathy somehow baked into their DNA. The ER team at Williamson Medical should seriously consider why they chose to serve the public. I wouldn't hire any of the nurses or the doctor we dealt with to deliver my mail - they'd find a way to screw it up. They might, however, be just right to pick up our trash curbside. To be fair, I should note we had generally positive experiences from the ER check-in staff. Also had acceptable treatment and care after getting my mother checked into the main hospital. But by the time we were upstairs, we had lost faith in the entire place, so we were watching/prodding them closely to be sure they attended properly to our mom. No one should need to do that. Later in the day I spoke to an EMT who said he wouldn't allow his friends or family to get taken to Williamson Medical ER, that they have an awful reputation as a dumping ground for patients who have no advocacy and no close family oversight. His quote was "tell them to take you farther north to Vandy, St. Thomas etc. ". He also said, "even if you arrive at Williamson Medical without an infection, you'll surely leave with one". Yikes. Wish I'd known. That's why I've labored over this review. Beware. And my heart goes out to anyone reading this who has a loved one suffering like my mother has. God bless.

text: Unfortunately I had a family member pass away last week and wanted a hotel close to the funeral home in White House, Tennessee. The hotel clerk was friendly and greeted me with a warm welcome. I personally called to make reservations in hopes of getting a first floor room. The room was a king, as requested, and the door had a clean, unbroken Covid-19 seal on it. The room had all the standard amenities except a microwave. Microwaves at this location are only in the suites. Who knew? I was quite disappointed but now know for my next trip. At least I had a cold mini fridge, functional TV, great water pressure, room darkening shades, an excellent air conditioner and a functioning blow dryer. The comfortable bed and pillows were clean and I didn't find any type of bugs. I check! Covid-19 guidelines are being enforced with masks required outside of your room, door seals, hand sanitizer at the front desk, lobby furniture has been removed and the hot breakfast buffet has been replaced with a brown bag breakfast (fruit, granola bar and yogurt to go). Cracker Barrel is within walking distance. Coffee pots are in each room if you need coffee or drive across the street to one of the fast food restaurants. The pool and workout situation requires a signed release, schedule your time (1 hour) through the front desk, receive your towel and off you go at your appointed time. I checked availability but they book quickly especially on the weekends. The hotel supplied everything I needed except a microwave. Of course having a relaxing, hot breakfast with coffee and no Covid-19 restrictions would have been convenient and a dream at this time. However, I think those days are probably gone. Regardless, I slept well, the room was clean, temperature was perfect for me and the staff was friendly. I'd stay here again.

text: Wow, what a bummer. I come to town often and had visited the old location probably 40 times over the last few years. The space was small, but the taps were many and well chosen. There was free shuffleboard. The bartenders were knowledgeable and provided great service, even during rushes. Small taster glasses were readily and patiently provided and suggestions from the bartenders were helpful, especially if something had run out. Sadly, it seems that the new space was designed to replace that experience with something that has less charm than visiting a Chipotle. There are still a good number of taps, but bartenders, and the entire concept of hands-on bar/beer service is just...gone. Replaced with "cashiers" and an order window. For beer. Seriously. The cashier on our recent visit was nice enough, and willing even to offer a 'taster' of a beer, but that was provided - no joke - in a disposable plastic 2 oz sauce cup....like something they would give you meds in in a hospital (or a side of ranch). Your opinions about the new location will probably depend entirely on why you liked the old location. If it was just to go in and eat, or grab food to go, you might not notice much difference. If you liked it as a beer destination - a place to try and learn about different beers with nice food service to boot - you will probably hate the sterile, low service approach of the new location. text: New Years day today and time to fulfill a yearly ritual to go out and eat some seafood,so based on positive Yelp reviews decided to visit Skidders. This place serves seafood,Italian and Greek food and normally I avoid places that serve many different types of food because they are usually mediocre across the board but it appears that Skidders is firing on all cylinders. The place was busy but we were seated quickly.We ordered drinks and appetizers and tried the fresh bread that was brought out.The bread was warm and quite tasty.The raspberry tea has just a hint of raspberry taste but the tea itself is good.The appetizers we ordered were the calamari,stuffed mushrooms and jalapeno poppers.All three were excellent,with decent sized servings,especially the calamari,which came with a fresh marinara type sauce. The wife and I both went for the fried combo platter which has flounder,shrimp and scallops with the standard sides of coleslaw and french fries.Deep frying seafood can be tricky,but our stuff was done just right,tender and not over or underdone.The fish was good,the shrimp better and the scallops best,The scallops were so delicious that I could have eaten a plate full of just them.They were large,tender and flavorful.The fries were plentiful but could of been warmer. Our waiter was attentive and kept us supplied with refills on our drinks,bread and also extra napkins when we requested them. All in all it was a good experience and a great way to start off the New Year.Everything went smoothly and nothing major to report in the negative department so I'm giving them 5 stars,It was our first visit and we plan on returning to try some of their yummy looking Italian and Greek dishes.

text: The Indiana Medical History Museum is located on the Central State Hospital Campus on West Vermont. This place is so cool if your a history buff, in the medical field or curious about the history of mental disease. So many stories and so much history to explore on the tour. Easy to find and parking isn't an issue. Note they are closed Sunday - Tuesday with open hours of 10a-4p, Wednesday through Saturday. The tour guides are very knowledgeable and friendly. The tours are approximately an hour and start on the hour. Doors are locked during a tour due to limited staff so arrive a few minutes before your tour. The last tour begins at 3:00 p.m. No reservations needed unless you are a group of 6 or more then call ahead preferably 3 weeks. The admission is only $10 for adults, $9 for seniors, $5 for college students with valid ID and only $3 for students under 18. Very affordable for families and groups plus an amazing amount of history surrounds you while hearing revealing, true stories. It definitely is a museum worth revisiting because it is difficult to catch and retain everything the first time through. The heart of the museum is the Old Pathology Building, the oldest surviving pathology facility in the nation. The Building is on the National Register of Historic Places. Inaugurated in 1896, the Pathological Department facilitated medical education and research on the physical causes of mental disease. In operation until the 1960s, the Pathological Department was reborn as a museum in 1969 and its scientifically equipped interior was left intact with several new pieces donated over the years. You'll view the Teaching Amphitheater, the Autopsy room where organ were retained to study, the Anatomical Museum and lab room, the Morgue, the Photography Room, the Clinical Laboratory and the Histology Lab to name a few. The doctors were diligently working to discover the causes of depression, dementia and schizophrenia. I was amazed at the number of interesting stories we heard and truly saw how much has changed in a 100 years. A very enjoyable and instructive tour plus they try to answer all questions if possible. I highly recommend if you're searching for something different to do for an hour even if you have no medical background. Are you an avid history buff? The tour is afforable, enjoyable and you'll appreciate how far our medical history has come in a 100 years. Note, not suitable for small children, those with issues of discussions concerning death, autopsies, or viewing body parts and skeletons. Some squeamish folks could have issues.

text: This week was my gf's birthday and I wanted to surprise her with a birthday dinner at a Peruvian restaurant because she had lived in Peru for a year and a half before I met her. The menu looked promising, so I called them up a week in advance and told them that there would be 13 of us and they made the reservation. Everyone kept the secret and arrived at the scheduled time (30 minutes before my gf and I arrived). We walked in everyone sang Happy Birthday and our wonderful evening began. My gf recognized some traditional Peruvian dishes and drinks on the menu, and they played some of her favorite Latino music (at a good volume level) throughout the evening over their speakers. We mostly shared appetizer and entree dishes because we wanted to try a variety of things. The entrees in particular were about family sized and we ended up having food leftover to take home. Everyone had at least one drink, most had two. There was only one waiter serving us and the rest of the restaurant, but he did a great job and was helpful in making menu selections. Some of the dishes had a spice that my gf has tried to find in STL but has struggled to find (the name escapes me - maybe aji?), and it is delicious (a little kick to it) - we asked the waiter where they get theirs from, and before we left (and after we had paid the bill) he gave us a whole large unopened jar of it. In summary, we had a great evening that was elevated by great food and service. For all 13 of us (again with about two drinks each and shared appetizers and entrees (some got their own entrees) the bill came out to only $34 person (with a 20% tip!). This is the first review I have written on Yelp (and may be my last) - I would definitely recommend this restaurant (I'd give it more stars if I could) and hope they do well!

text: The Hank's Manifesto By Dr M Herzberg A neighborhood can be compared to a living organism. Its streets are the veins, its homes are the skin, its trees and plants are the lungs, and its many varied inhabitants are the brain and central nervous system. But as any scientist (such as myself) can tell you, no organism can survive without a heart. In the case of the organism that is the Marigny/Bywater, Hank's fulfills that role. This is true on a physical level: Hank's moves our bloodstream by providing it with precious resources such as 40's of malt beverages, corn dogs, "tobacco" pipes, Roquefort cheese, canned beans, etcetera. But more importantly, Hank's is the neighborhood's spiritual heart. People come to Hank's from all walks of life to heal, to escape the nihilist horror and alienation which day-to-day life in our capitalist society inevitably accompany. Hank's cares not whether you have won today's battle with your inner daemons or whether guilt and shame consumes you. Hank's is here for you to listen, without judgement, and to bless your broken soul. Yes, they were allegedly anti-semites, back in days of yore. That's a big no-no. But this era of hatred has passed, as the employees who perpetrated these vile injustices have been tried and punished in the international court of Hank's. The banality of evil has been replaced with the totality of love and understanding. The new Hankers are people of honor and integrity, and they will hold your head on their bosoms and sing their sweet lullabies as you weep your tears of sorrow, washing away years of emotional repression and resentment. The pressing question remains: who is Hank? Is Hank the owner who benevolently smiles at us from his hidden palace? Is Hank the lady who makes the fried chicken in disguise? Is Hank the crusty in the parking lot who asks you for 47 cents? Hank remains a misunderstood figure, because in truth, there is no one Hank. Hank is an ethereal concept: we are all Hank. As such I invite you to see for yourself the greatest organization in this country, nay, on this planet. Be it for an afternoon shrimp po-boy (with extra hot sauce) or a handjob in the parking lot (not officially endorsed by Hank's, but they'll provide you with lube and napkins), come and awaken your inner ubermensch as you do away with the corpse of Judeo-Christian morality and see the truth beyond good and evil: Hank.

text: The Columbia Restaurant in Ybor is a Tampa tradition. I know that there are locations all over Florida, but this one is special. It has been here for over a hundred years and on the spot where Theodore Roosevelt and his Rough Riders watered their horses. If you want the Tampa experience, look no further than The Columbia. It is a combination of Spanish and Cuban food, prepared in a special atmospheric style. Their staff is wonderfully polite and cordial. You may have to wait a bit, depending on the time and whether or not you made reservations. The wait is worth it. Appetizers are phenomenal- everyone is served with hot Cuban Bread and butter ( oh so wonderful). My favorite appetizer here is probably the garbanzo bean soup. It has a fantastically smoky flavor. I would also recommend a pitcher of their sangria to share with friends- it is the best I have had in a restaurant. For entrees I would recommend their rope vieja ( shredded pork on white rice), boliche ( tender beef with chorizo in the middle served with rice), arroz con pollo ( chicken with rice), or one of their many paella dishes. As a good friend put it, all you have to do is point on the menu and you'll enjoy your order. To finish, get either a Cafe con Leche or a fresh brewed coffee. My personal favorite is the guava turnover - not too sweet and delightfully crisp. The Columbia's flan and creme brûlée's are also amazing. Above all remember, this is an experience, so bring friends and enjoy.

She is also a decorated doctor who continues to pursue education throughout her career, specifically with regards to gender affirmation surgery. As a queer and trans person, it can be really difficult to find a doctor and team in the Midwest (much less, right here in Saint Louis) who is all of the following: highly skilled in the different types of top surgery, compassionate, confident, aware and sensitive to pronouns and other gender related issues that are relevant when you're getting top surgery. Dr. McGuire knows that different trans and gender non conforming folks who pursue top surgery have different goals with their chest. For me, I was looking for a surgeon who understood that top surgery is more than just removing breast tissue. Dr. McGuire understands that and assured me that she would help masculinize my chest. Trusting someone with your body, and as a trans person trusting someone with the reconstruction of your chest is a huge deal. I am so glad I trusted Dr. McGuire with mine. Her bed side manner is exactly what you'd want in a surgeon: professional, highly confident, with super positive energy. When I left Dr. McGuire's office after my consult, I knew she would be my surgeon. Here's why: It can be easy for such intelligent and skilled people to overlook the importance of sensitivity, especially when it comes to working with folks who are trans. Not only was Dr. McGuire sensitive to my pronouns, but also generally aware of gender dysphoria, which can make going to the doctor, talking about your body, letting others see your body difficult and complicated. Throughout the process my comfort level was a priority. I had great vibes about her from the moment I met her. It's not just her, it's the whole team. text: You can often tell if an authentic Chinese restaurant is worth its salt by a few markers. Does it offer a character-appropriate, bilingual menu? Check. Does it have tried and true boba tea offerings, even fare like honey lemon tea? Check. Does it have at least one English misspelling on the menu displayed at the front but a clever Chinese idiom name? Double check. You know you're in a great, not good, place when the staff has thoughtfully placed electric buttons for service in the corner, disposable napkins dispensed like tissues on the table, and encased the tablecloths in glass. Now, what to order? Honestly, anything off of the noodle menu. It is, after all, a noodle house. The Chongqing Noodles are the restaurant's namesake, so I suggest either the house favorite or Zhou's beef noodle soup. I admit, the quality of the noodles themselves are a bit wanting. I highly recommend handpulled noodles, but you are yet to unlockthat particular level in the Nashville area. Given that competition is relatively low in Nashville for proper Chinese fare, this is by far one of the best noodle shops given its outstanding (albeit still relatively high) price point. When a restaurant has cheese milk foam drinks on its menu in the South, you have to hope for nothing but its success. Nashville's international student population needs this. Honestly, Nashville locals need this injection of culture. I'm not saying this is the next Din Tai Fung or Kung Fu Tea. However, at a local level with low competition? Meet Noodles blows everything else out of the water. Just make sure to order in Chinese or order with someone who can to get the full, proper cuisine experience.

text: We stopped in after making reservations for an early Saturday evening dinner. Overall, we had good food, generous portions, and a pleasant server. However, there were a few things about the place that could use some attention. After parking in the Circle Centre Mall, we strolled down Meridian and entered. The interior of the restaurant is broken into lots of small rooms and a bar that you can partially see from the entry. There is also a Host lectern that was unmanned, so we waited a couple minutes for anyone of the staff to greet us. I don't understand the point of having a station for a host and not having anyone there. But since we had reservations, someone eventually arrived and seated us to the right in one of the small rooms. We waited a few minutes and our waitress arrived and took our beverage orders. We watched as two other couples arrived and left because no one was there to greet them. Some other people arrived and seated themselves at the bar. It was becoming a pattern of confusion about seating. After our beverages arrive, we quickly placed our orders to make sure the food was put in the queue. Although we never had that long to wait, we rarely saw any staff during the visit because of our secluded room. It felt odd. By mid-meal, we noticed that one of the male servers was telling guests that there was a 30 minute wait. We had a 6-person table in our nook that was unfilled and I could see a 4-person table unused across the way. Did they simply not have enough staff to man the tables? Again, it seemed like a lost revenue opportunity for the restaurant because ALL the customers who were told of the delay left. Fortunately, our food arrived in a timely fashion and it was quite good. I had a starter cup of Guinness Onion Soup that had a delightful flavor. There wasn't any actual broth since their version has garlic bread cubes in the soup that absorbed all the broth. The onions were so cooked that they were there in flavor, but not visible (they must have completely broken down into the broth.) The cheese topping was melted and easy to dig through with a spoon which made eating the soup very easy. Really good flavor. The only real negative was that the house bread was a bit dry and without any broth to dip it in, it was less than I had hoped. I also ordered the fish 'n chips. A large single piece of battered white fish came with lots of seasoned potato wedges, cole slaw, and tartar sauce. Good flavor without being overcooked made for a filling meal. Note that they do have malt vinegar on the tables for those who prefer it to tartar sauce. My wife got the Paddy Mac Sandwich with the corned beef replaced by smoked turkey. It comes with cole slaw on the sandwich along with Swiss cheese, 1000 Island dressing and served on marbled rye and a side of the potato wedges. She thought the flavor was pretty good but though the ratio of turkey to cole slaw was light on the turkey. As I mentioned above, we enjoyed our meal and found our server to be pleasant though some small delays occurred. I hope they can use this review to address the lack of a greeting to customers who are coming in out of the cold and have nobody to talk to. Review #3332

text: While in the area shopping, my grandmother had some extra time so we stopped in to A Taste of Britain for afternoon tea. Luckily they were able to accommodate us and we were seated within 10 minutes of arrival. Our server was great. Plus we received the tea sandwiches for the day (roast beef and horsey, vegetable cream cheese, tuna salad, and egg salad). I'm not a huge meat person but the roast beef and horsey was my favorite; my least favorite was the vegetable cream cheese (the ratio of cream cheese to bread was too much in my opinion). The portion size was generous (8 tea sandwiches) for the afternoon tea. The scones were good and served slightly warmed. I love that they have lemon curd (as well as the normal clotted cream and jam) to accompany the scones (you'd be surprised at how many tea rooms don't serve lemon curd!). Desserts were also included however they were very vanilla heavy (vanilla cake with vanilla icing, vanilla mini cupcake with vanilla icing, cheesecake brownie bite). So for the full afternoon tea ($22), you receive a pot of tea (about 2.5 cups), 8 tea sandwiches, a scone of your choice, and an assortment of desserts which is definitely reasonable for the price. I'd come back again for sure!
